title: Understanding Cognitive Dissonance
text:
Cognitive dissonance theory posits that humans strive for internal consistency among their beliefs, values, and actions. When an individual holds two or more conflicting cognitions—for example, knowing smoking is harmful while continuing to smoke—it creates a state of mental discomfort, known as dissonance.

The intensity of this psychological distress is proportional to the importance of the cognitions involved and the discrepancy between them. Because this uncomfortable state cannot be maintained long-term, individuals are motivated to reduce it by changing one or more elements of their cognitive structure.

Reduction can occur through several mechanisms: altering the behavior (quitting smoking), adjusting the belief (downplaying the risks of smoking), or adding new consonant cognitions to rationalize the conflict. The resulting rationalization often serves to restore a sense of mental equilibrium, even if the change is not logically sound.
